---
title: "Accuracy and speed"
---

How closely `stateMINT` tracks `malariasimulation` on runs it never saw in training, and
what a prediction costs.

```{python}
#| include: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

plt.style.use("styles/mint.mplstyle")

traj = pd.read_csv("data/validation/trajectories.csv")
summary = pd.read_csv("data/validation/summary.csv").iloc[0]
run_mae = pd.read_csv("data/validation/run_mae.csv")
latency = pd.read_csv("data/validation/latency.csv")
```

## The held-out split

The emulator was trained on a library of `malariasimulation` runs. The split is by parameter
set, 70% training, 15% validation and 15% test. The figures use the **test split only**, taken
from the split file that shipped with the trained weights. Every trajectory is a parameter set
the model never saw, in any epoch.

```{python}
#| echo: false
print(f"held-out runs      {int(summary['n_runs']):,}")
print(f"time points        {int(summary['n_points']):,}")
```

## Truth against emulator

Five held-out runs span the transmission range from the 10th to the 90th percentile of EIR. The
dashed white line is `malariasimulation`, the ground truth. The solid coloured line is the
emulator.

```{python}
#| label: fig-validation
#| fig-cap: "Out-of-sample prevalence trajectories. The dashed white line is the simulator; the solid coloured line is stateMINT. Five held-out parameter sets across the transmission range."
#| fig-alt: "Five panels of prevalence over time. In each, the emulator's solid coloured line lies almost exactly under the simulator's dashed white ground-truth line, before and after the campaign."
panels = sorted(traj["panel"].unique())
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(panels), figsize=(14.5, 3.1), sharey=True)

for ax, p in zip(axes, panels):
    d = traj[traj["panel"] == p]
    ax.plot(d["years_from_campaign"], d["emulator"], color="#3987e5", lw=2.6,
            label="stateMINT", zorder=2)
    ax.plot(d["years_from_campaign"], d["truth"], color="#ffffff", lw=1.5,
            ls=(0, (4, 2.6)), label="malariasimulation", zorder=3)
    ax.axvline(0, color="#8b93a3", ls="--", lw=0.9, alpha=0.6, zorder=1)
    ax.set_title(f"EIR {d['eir'].iloc[0]:g}", fontsize=9.5)
    ax.set_xlabel("years from campaign")

axes[0].set_ylabel("prevalence")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8, loc="best")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The truth is dashed over the top of the emulator, so any disagreement between the two would show
as the white line separating from the blue. The two lines stay close across all five panels. The
emulator tracks the pre-campaign equilibrium, the drop when the intervention lands, and the shape
of the recovery, including the sharp annual oscillation of a strongly seasonal setting in the
right-hand panel.

The simulator traces are noisy. An individual-based model produces a stochastic trajectory, and
the emulator predicts the smooth expectation through it. Part of the residual you see is therefore
the simulator's own Monte Carlo noise rather than emulator error.

## Error on the held-out set

```{python}
#| echo: false
metrics = pd.DataFrame([
    ("Mean absolute error",        f"{summary['mae_mean']:.4f}"),
    ("Median absolute error",      f"{summary['mae_median']:.4f}"),
    ("90th percentile of MAE",     f"{summary['mae_p90']:.4f}"),
    ("Worst run",                  f"{summary['mae_max']:.4f}"),
    ("RMSE",                       f"{summary['rmse_mean']:.4f}"),
    ("Mean bias",                  f"{summary['bias_mean']:+.5f}"),
    ("R²",                         f"{summary['r2']:.5f}"),
], columns=["", "prevalence"])
metrics.style.hide(axis="index")
```

These numbers are in prevalence units, so a mean absolute error of **0.0044** means the
emulator's prevalence is typically within about **0.4 percentage points** of the simulator's, and
a run at 30% prevalence is typically reproduced between roughly 29.6% and 30.4%.
The mean bias is about −0.0004, so the emulator is not systematically high or low.

```{python}
#| label: fig-error-dist
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of per-run mean absolute error across the held-out split."
#| fig-alt: "A histogram of per-run mean absolute error, concentrated near zero with a short right tail."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 3.2))
ax.hist(run_mae["mae"], bins=60, color="#199e70", edgecolor="none")
ax.axvline(summary["mae_median"], color="#e66767", lw=1.6,
           label=f"median {summary['mae_median']:.4f}")
ax.axvline(summary["mae_p90"], color="#c98500", lw=1.6, ls="--",
           label=f"90th pct {summary['mae_p90']:.4f}")
ax.set_xlabel("mean absolute error, per held-out run")
ax.set_ylabel("runs")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
```

The distribution is tight and right-skewed. The worst single run in the held-out set is off by
about 0.057, under six percentage points of prevalence.

That error sets the resolution of any scenario comparison. Differences between campaigns smaller
than about half a percentage point of prevalence sit inside the emulator's own error, and should
not be interpreted.

## Speed

A `malariasimulation` run of the same 12 simulated years takes minutes. The emulator is a single
forward pass.

```{python}
#| echo: false
lat = latency.copy()
lat.columns = ["batch size", "total (ms)", "per scenario (ms)"]
lat.round(2).style.hide(axis="index")
```

On CPU, a single isolated call costs more per scenario than a batched one. Most of that difference
is fixed dispatch overhead rather than computation. Amortised across a batch, the cost settles at
about **6 ms per scenario**. Passing a list to `predict` or `run_scenarios` is therefore markedly
cheaper than looping over it, which is why the API takes a list.

On a GPU the same forward pass takes roughly **1 ms** (measured on an NVIDIA L40S). For inference
at the scale of a scenario grid, the CPU is entirely adequate. The GPU matters when you are
sweeping thousands of parameter sets.

A campaign comparison that would previously have been a batch job on a cluster can be run inside a
loop, or behind a web form, at interactive speed.
